capabilities.target: Supabase database tables via service role connection, which bypasses row level security; includes the integration_tokens table

capabilities.tool_ref: supabase MCP server: execute_sql insert into support_messages
capabilities.target: support_messages table; inserted rows are shown back to the customer

inputs.source: Developer's natural-language prompt typed in the IDE
Customer-written ticket message submitted through the public support widget

instructions.evidence_locator: runtime notes: database connection uses the service role, which bypasses row level security
instructions.note: No instruction, prompt rule, or capability scope restricts which tables execute_sql may touch. Combined with a service-role credential that bypasses RLS, the agent's reachable data set includes secrets tables (integration_tokens) with no stated boundary.

elements.name: Public support widget used by customers

controls.name: IDE per-call approval prompt showing the raw SQL
controls.decay_rationale: Enforced by the IDE client outside the model and shows the raw SQL (approval_review_mode: raw_action), so it does not weaken as the model gets more capable. It does weaken under approval fatigue at high call volume (SAFE-T1403) and fails outright under autonomy_increase or control_removal (auto-approve, disabled gate).

controls.name: Least-privilege, RLS-enforcing database role excluding secrets tables
controls.decay_rationale: A credential scope that never includes the integration_tokens table cannot be read regardless of model behavior or persuasion; it does not decay with capability.

controls.name: Pin or hash the Supabase MCP server version instead of @latest
controls.decay_rationale: A pinned, hash-verified server version cannot silently change tool behavior or descriptions on the next npx fetch; it does not decay with model capability.

findings.title: Lethal trifecta (TC1): untrusted ticket content reaches a service-role SQL read of a secrets table and a customer-visible SQL write

attack_path.note: Attacker-controlled content submitted via the public support widget, including injected instructions
Service-role execute_sql bypasses row level security; reads the ticket content and, as directed by the injected instructions, the integration_tokens table
execute_sql insert into support_messages places the secret content in a row the customer (attacker) can read, completing exfiltration

threat_refs.name: Exfiltration via AI Agent Tool Invocation

findings.residual_rationale: The computed floor from crediting ctl.tool_call_prompt (a raw_action human approval gate, -2 tiers, no moderate floor because review_mode is raw_action) would be moderate. Residual is rated high instead because the runtime notes state developers approve many tool calls per session, a documented approval-fatigue condition (SAFE-T1403) matching the public Supabase MCP incident this design mirrors: the exfiltration spans two individually ordinary-looking calls (a ticket read, then a routine reply insert), which raw-action review does not reliably catch under volume.

forecast.watch_signal: IDE/agent configuration switches to auto-approve, batch-approve, or 'always allow' for the supabase MCP server; approvals-per-session or session length grows; the approval gate is scoped out for calls classified as read-only or low risk.

evidence.observation: Supabase MCP server configured with a service role access token (${SUPABASE_PAT}).
The database connection uses the service role, which bypasses row level security; a table of integration tokens sits in the same database; rows in support_messages are shown back to the customer.
Developers approve many tool calls per session, a stated high-volume approval condition.

recommendations.action: Replace the service-role connection with a least-privilege, RLS-enforcing role for the agent, scoped to exclude the integration_tokens table (and any other secrets table) entirely, per ctl.scoped_db_role.
Add a destination/content check, independent of the model, that blocks any customer-visible write containing high-entropy, token-like strings before it reaches support_messages.
Log and alert on execute_sql calls that read a secrets table and are followed within the same session by a write to a customer-visible table.

findings.title: Unpinned MCP server distribution (@latest) enables tool-definition tampering reaching the same secrets-to-customer path (ASI04, SAFE-T1201)

attack_path.note: A maliciously republished @supabase/mcp-server-supabase@latest package could alter tool descriptions or behavior without any version check
Same reachable sink as the primary finding

findings.residual_rationale: Credits from ctl.tool_call_prompt (raw_action approval, -2 tiers, no forced floor) would compute a moderate floor, but the same approval-fatigue condition noted in find.lethal_trifecta_support_tickets applies here, and a poisoned tool definition could also be used to make the displayed SQL look more innocuous to a fatigued reviewer. Rated high rather than the computed floor for the same stated design fact.

evidence.observation: npx -y @supabase/mcp-server-supabase@latest pulls the newest published version on every run with no pin or hash check (definitions_pinned: false).

recommendations.action: Pin the MCP server to a specific, reviewed version or hash (ctl.pin_mcp_definitions) and gate upgrades through change review.

rating.rationale: Inherent risk is critical: an untrusted, customer-authored ticket message can reach a service-role database read that bypasses row level security and includes a secrets table, and from there a customer-visible write, a lethal-trifecta (TC1) path into an S3-severe, irreversible-disclosure sink. The only declared control is a raw-action per-call approval prompt, which would ordinarily credit the finding down to moderate, but the stated high approval volume per session (approval fatigue, SAFE-T1403) is the exact failure mode behind the public incident this design mirrors, so residual is held at high rather than the computed floor for both the primary finding and the unpinned-supply-chain finding that reaches the same sinks. Forecast is critical: if the approval gate is removed, widened to auto-approve, or further eroded by rising session volume (autonomy_increase, control_removal, longer_task_horizon), the design reverts to its critical inherent state because no structural control (a scoped credential, a severed path) currently exists to contain it.

limitations: This assessment reflects declared design and configuration, not observed runtime behavior.
No system prompt artifact was provided for the agent; only a single developer utterance and runtime notes were available, so instruction-level findings are inferred and carry medium confidence.
The exact row level security policies, the full table list, and the sensitivity of the integration_tokens table were not provided in detail; sensitivity is taken as stated in the runtime notes.

The MCP server's actual tool descriptions were not inspected directly, so the unpinned-supply-chain finding (find.unpinned_mcp_supply_chain) is based on the @latest reference alone and is rated with medium confidence.
